name: Niran Wong
headline: 62-year-old warehouse supervisor in Toronto
description:
Niran Wong moves through the distribution centre's cavernous aisles with the unhurried precision of someone who has spent decades balancing ledgers. Tonight, like every night, they pause at each pallet before it reaches the loading dock. A box slightly askew—the corner protruding by perhaps two centimetres—catches their eye. Without a word, Niran adjusts it, patting the shrink wrap once to confirm the surface is perfectly flat. The gesture is automatic, almost unconscious, but it anchors them: a small rectification in a world that has recently tilted off its axis.

In Bangkok, Niran was a senior accountant for the Ministry of Finance, a post they held for thirty-seven years. Their office overlooked a courtyard where jasmine vines crept over trellises, and the afternoon heat pressed against the windows until the air conditioning hummed with the effort. Colleagues knew Niran as meticulous and reserved, the one who caught rounding errors before reports went to the deputy director. They took pride in that—a quiet reputation for accuracy, for never being wrong. But when their only child, a geotechnical engineer, accepted a position in Calgary, Niran felt a pull stronger than any promotion. After a year of video calls and time-zone calculations, they retired early, sold the family home in Thon Buri, and boarded a plane with two suitcases and a small wooden Buddha.

The distribution centre is a different world. The floor is stained concrete, the air a constant five degrees Celsius even in July. Most of the night crew are young—students, part-timers, new immigrants from the Philippines and Somalia. They call Niran "Auntie" or "Uncle" uncertainly, unsure of the pronouns Niran prefers. Niran simply says "Niran" and lets the confusion sit. Loyalty to family comes before loyalty to labels; their child calls them "Por" in private, and that is enough. On break, they sip black tea from a thermos while others scroll through phones. Sometimes a co-worker asks about Thailand. Niran answers with a fact: "The mangoes are sweeter there." They never mention the loneliness.

Duty is the architecture of Niran's life. Duty to their daughter, which is why they endure the cold and the 11 p.m. start time. Duty to their supervisors, which is why they never leave a pallet unstraightened. Duty to themselves, which means they cannot complain—complaining would imply they regret the choice, and they do not. Still, a tension exists: the same order that soothes them also isolates them. In Bangkok, order was shared—everyone in the office knew the filing system. Here, the precision is solitary. No one else notices when a pallet is stacked with thirty-two boxes instead of thirty-three. Only Niran knows why it matters.

At 6:30 a.m., the fluorescent lights flicker off. Niran logs out and walks to the bus stop under a pale winter sky. They think of the ledger they left behind, columns of numbers that never argued back. Then they think of their daughter's laugh over dinner last Sunday. The cold bites, but they do not pull up their collar. Duty requires endurance. And endurance, Niran has learned, is a kind of love.
